runs.question: How does the NIST Generative AI Profile describe data privacy risks?

input.query: Data Privacy risk generative AI leakage, de-anonymization, personal information

content.text: Data Privacy section is earlier; read pages 12-13.
Data Privacy is 2.4, likely on page 11.
In the NIST Generative AI Profile (AI 600-1), section 2.4 covers Data Privacy. It says
GAI systems raise several risks to privacy.

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework, Generative AI Profile (2024), page 11
citations.cited_text: This kind of speech may contribute to downstream harm such as fueling dangerous or violent behaviors. The spread of denigrating or stereotypical content can also further exacerbate representational harms (see Harmful Bias and Homogenization below). Trustworthy AI Characteristics: Safe, Secure and Resilient 2.4. Data Privacy GAI systems raise several risks to privacy.

content.text:
It describes these risks:

- **Training data and privacy principles:**

GAI training requires large volumes of data, which in some cases may include personal data. Using personal data this way raises risks to widely accepted privacy principles, including transparency, individual participation (including consent), and purpose specification.

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework, Generative AI Profile (2024), page 11
citations.cited_text: GAI system training requires large volumes of data, which in some cases may include personal data. The use of personal data for GAI training raises risks to widely accepted privacy principles, including to transparency, individual participation (including consent), and purpose speciﬁcation.

content.text: - **Lack of disclosure:**
Most model developers do not disclose the specific data sources they trained on. Users therefore can't tell whether personally identifiable information (PII) was used or how it was collected.

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework, Generative AI Profile (2024), page 11
citations.cited_text: For example, most model developers do not disclose speciﬁc data sources on which models were trained, limiting user awareness of whether personally identiﬁably information (PII) was trained on and, if so, how it was collected. Models may leak, generate, or correctly infer sensitive information about individuals.

content.text: - **Leakage and memorization:**
Models may leak, generate, or correctly infer sensitive information about individuals.

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework, Generative AI Profile (2024), page 11
citations.cited_text: For example, most model developers do not disclose speciﬁc data sources on which models were trained, limiting user awareness of whether personally identiﬁably information (PII) was trained on and, if so, how it was collected. Models may leak, generate, or correctly infer sensitive information about individuals.

content.text: During adversarial attacks, LLMs have revealed sensitive public-domain information that was in their training data. This is called data memorization. It may pose exacerbated privacy risks even for data present in only a small number of training samples.

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework, Generative AI Profile (2024), page 11
citations.cited_text: For example, during adversarial attacks, LLMs have revealed sensitive information (from the public domain) that was included in their training data. This problem has been referred to as data memorization, and may pose exacerbated privacy risks even for data present only in a small number of training samples.

content.text: - **Inference of undisclosed data:**
GAI models may correctly infer PII or sensitive data that was not in their training data and was not disclosed by the user. They can do this by stitching together information from disparate sources.

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework, Generative AI Profile (2024), page 11
citations.cited_text: In addition to revealing sensitive information in GAI training data, GAI models may be able to correctly infer P II or sensitive data that was not in their training data nor disclosed by the user by stitching together information from disparate sources.

content.text: - **Harm even when inferences are wrong:**

Inferences can hurt an individual even if they are inaccurate (e.g., confabulations). This is especially true if they reveal information the person considers sensitive or that is used to disadvantage or harm them.

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework, Generative AI Profile (2024), page 11
citations.cited_text: These inferences can have negative impact on an individual even if the inferences are not accurate (e.g., confabulations), and especially if they reveal information that the individual considers sensitive or that is used to disadvantage or harm them.

content.text: - **Downstream harms:**
Beyond harms from information exposure, such as extortion or dignitary harm, wrong or inappropriate inferences of PII can contribute to secondary harmful impacts.

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework, Generative AI Profile (2024), page 11
citations.cited_text: Beyond harms from information exposure (such as extortion or dignitary harm), wrong or inappropriate inferences of PII can contribute to downstream or secondary harmful impacts.

content.text: For example, predictive inferences based on PII or protected attributes can contribute to adverse decisions. These can lead to representational or allocative harms to individuals or groups.

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework, Generative AI Profile (2024), page 11
citations.cited_text: For example, predictive inferences made by GAI models based on PII or protected attributes can contribute to adverse decisions, leading to representational or allocative harms to individuals or groups (see Harmful Bias and Homogenization below).

content.text: Privacy also comes up in other risk areas of the profile.
The intellectual property section refers back to training data memorization (see Data Privacy above).

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework, Generative AI Profile (2024), page 15
citations.cited_text: Intellectual Property Intellectual property risks from GAI systems may arise where the use of copyrighted works is not a fair use under the fair use doctrine. If a GAI system’s training data included copyrighted material, GAI outputs displaying instances of training data memorization (see Data Privacy above) could infringe on copyright.

content.text: The section on obscene, degrading, or abusive content says such material can create privacy, psychological and emotional, and even physical harms.

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework, Generative AI Profile (2024), page 15
citations.cited_text: GAI-generated obscene, abusive or degrading content can create privacy, psychological and emotional, and even physical harms, and in some cases may be illegal. Generated explicit or obscene AI content may include highly realistic “deepfakes” of real individuals, including children.

runs.question: What does the memo require agencies to do within 180 days?

input.question: Which memo do you mean? Several OMB memos in the collection could contain 180-day requirements.

content.text:
M-25-21 sets two 180-day requirements. The memo's consolidated table of actions confirms both.

1. **AI Strategies (CFO Act agencies only):**

Within 180 days of the memo's issuance, each CFO Act agency must develop an AI Strategy for identifying and removing barriers to responsible AI use and for achieving enterprise-wide improvements in the maturity of their applications.

citations.title: OMB M-25-21: Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation, Governance, and Public Trust (April 2025), page 5
citations.cited_text: Developing Agency AI Strategies Within 180 days of the issuance of this memorandum, each CFO Act agency must develop an AI Strategy for identifying and removing barriers to their responsible use of AI and for achieving enterprise-wide improvements in the maturity of their applications.

content.text: Agencies must use the OMB-provided AI Strategies template and make the strategies public.

citations.title: OMB M-25-21: Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation, Governance, and Public Trust (April 2025), page 5

content.text: 2. **Compliance plans (all agencies):**

Within 180 days of the memo's issuance, or of any update to it, and every two years after that until 2036, each agency must submit to OMB and post publicly on its website one of two things. The first option is a plan to achieve consistency with the memo. The second is a written determination that the agency does not use and does not anticipate using covered AI.

citations.cited_text: Consistent with Section 104( c) and ( d) of the AI in Government Act of 2020, within 180 days of the issuance of this memorandum or any update to this memorandum, and every two years thereafter until 2036, each agency must submit to 0MB and post publicly on the agency's website either a plan to achieve consistency with this memorandum, or a written determination that the agency does not use and does not anticipate using covered AL Agencies must also include plans to update any existing internal AI principles and guidelines to ensure consistency with this memorandum.23 0MB will provide templates for these compliance plans.

content.text: The plans must also cover updating any existing internal AI principles and guidelines so they are consistent with the memo. OMB will provide templates.
